case_title: Paulmeli and Anr. v. State of Tamil Nadu
accused_victim_relationship: Relative (the State said the parties were closely related); prior enmity between the two families, as described in the prosecution case
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (conviction); FIR also registered under IPC ss.147, 148, 324, 326, 307
weapon: Aruval (machete-type cutting weapon, as named in the judgment)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (victim's wife, PW.1; hostile son PW.2 in part); medical (post-mortem by PW.11 and injury certificates); recovery on disclosure statements; FIR; mahazar; electricity supply evidence
confession: None (recoveries were made on disclosure statements, but no confession was relied on)
aggravating_circumstances: Indiscriminate multiple cut wounds by an armed group; injuries also caused to the victim's two sons who intervened
trial_court_outcome: On fresh trial, convicted the two accused under IPC s.302 and sentenced each to life imprisonment and a fine of Rs.2,000 (default six months RI); other accused acquitted
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
neutral_facts: Some twenty years after an earlier family dispute, which had caused enmity between two families, a group of seventeen persons, including the two accused, allegedly assembled with the common object of killing the victim. On the night of 30 July 1999, the victim was sleeping on a cot outside his house. The assailants allegedly encircled him and inflicted indiscriminate cuts over his body with an aruval, causing instant death. The victim's two sons intervened to save him and were also injured. After the attack the assailants ran away. The matter was first reported to a police station whose jurisdiction did not cover the place of occurrence. An inspector went to the scene that night and recorded the statement of the victim's wife, and a first information report was registered the next morning. The post-mortem examination recorded fifteen incised wounds, mainly on the neck, chest, shoulder, arm and hand. The victim's two sons were also treated for cut injuries. The victim's wife testified that she had known both accused for a long time because they were closely related, and that she recognised them even though it was dark, relying on a street light and electricity supply at the scene. One injured son initially did not support the prosecution but, when examined, named the two accused as taking part in the attack. A wireman from the electricity board gave evidence that power was supplied at the scene at the relevant time. Recoveries were made on the basis of the accused's disclosure statements.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from multiple incised wounds (post-mortem recorded fifteen wounds on neck, chest, shoulder, arm and hand); victim's two sons injured
premeditation_planning: Not stated: the court made no finding on premeditation; the common object to murder was alleged by the prosecution
motive: alleged: long-standing enmity between the two families arising from the desertion of a woman related to the victim; the Court did not decide the motive
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness account of the victim's wife (PW.1) naming both appellants; post-mortem and injury evidence corroborating her; prompt FIR; the hostile son's (PW.2) evidence against the appellants; evidence on light at the scene
witness_credibility: PW.1 found credible and identification accepted despite discrepancy about light, the court excusing it given her illiteracy and familiarity with the accused; PW.2 hostile but his evidence against the appellants accepted; PW.3 not independent but not discredited; the doctor was not cross-examined on injuries
post_offence_conduct: Ran away after the offence (prosecution case); the Court did not separately discuss it
trial_duration: offence: 30.7.1999; trial judgment: 18.11.2008 (fresh trial; earlier acquittal dated 27.11.2001); High Court: 6.10.2009; Supreme Court: 23 May 2014
legal_representation: Shirin Khajuria for the appellants; M. Yogesh Kanna for the State (respondent)
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; chargesheet filed against 17 accused; case committed to Sessions Court; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: None noted by the Court as a lapse by the authorities; the defence's failure to cross-examine the doctor on injuries was held against it
appeal_history: Trial court (first trial): all accused acquitted on 27.11.2001; revision by complainant allowed and retrial ordered; retrial court convicted the two appellants under s.302 IPC on 18.11.2008; High Court dismissed appeal on 6.10.2009; Supreme Court dismissed appeal
prosecution_argument: Parties closely related; PW.2 turned hostile but named the appellants in examination-in-chief; sufficient light and PW.1 could identify them; discrepancies insignificant; acquittal of others does not help the appellants
defence_argument: Evidence disbelieved for other accused cannot support conviction; PW.2 did not support the prosecution; complete darkness so PW.1 could not identify the appellants; material discrepancies in the manner and number of injuries
legal_principle_applied: Evidence of a hostile witness may be accepted in part; separate grain from chaff; falsus in uno principle not applicable; failure to cross-examine a witness on a point bars raising it later
precedent_relied_upon: Atluri Brahmanandam v. Anne Sai Bapuji, AIR 2011 SC 545; Laxmibai v. Bhagwantbuva, AIR 2013 SC 1204; Ramesh Harijan v. State of UP, AIR 2012 SC 1979; State of UP v. Ramesh Prasad Misra, AIR 1996 SC 2766; Sarvesh Narain Shukla v. Daroga Singh, AIR 2008 SC 320; Subbu Singh v. State, (2009) 6 SCC 462; C. Muniappan v. State of Tamil Nadu, AIR 2010 SC 3718; Himanshu @ Chintu v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2011) 2 SCC 36; Balka Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1975 SC 1962; Zwinglee Ariel v. State of MP, AIR 1954 SC 15; Sukhdev Yadav v. State of Bihar, AIR 2001 SC 3678; Appabhai v. State of Gujarat, AIR 1988 SC 696; Sucha Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 2003 SC 3617
